477.title: Masei: one date of death (Numbers 33:38)
477.hook: the only death the Torah dates exactly is Aaron's
477.howItsDone: Jews mark the yahrzeit, the anniversary of a death by the Hebrew calendar, by lighting a candle that burns for a full day, saying the mourner's Kaddish, and often giving charity in the person's memory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Masei, the journeys, with every stop on the road named, even the forgettable ones. Your line was every stop counts. Which places from your life did you remember? Day four hundred seventy-seven.

Some dates live in your phone's calendar. Others live in your body. You feel them coming before you check: the week your father died, the day the house burned, the anniversary nobody else remembers. Many families keep those dates carefully, year after year. In the middle of yesterday's long list of campsites, the Torah stops. Between one station and the next, it pauses for a death. And it does something it does for no one else: it gives the exact date.
screen: `DATES THAT LIVE IN THE BODY.` → `THE LIST STOPS FOR A DEATH.` → `THE EXACT DATE.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. Aaron the priest went up Mount Hor at the Lord's command and died there, in the fortieth year after the children of Israel came out of Egypt, in the fifth month, on the first day of the month. Then: Aaron was a hundred and twenty-three years old when he died on Mount Hor. Year, month, day and age. Readers have long noticed that this is the only death in the Torah given a full date like this. Even Moses' death, at the end of Deuteronomy, comes without a date. The rabbis later worked out a traditional date for Moses, the seventh of Adar, by calculating from other verses, but the Torah itself doesn't say. For Aaron, it does. The fifth month in the Torah's counting is the month later called Av. So Aaron died on the first of Av, the start of the saddest month of the Jewish year. The Torah had already told the story of his death back in Chukat; here it marks the day. Why? The text doesn't explain. But Jewish life has kept the instinct. The anniversary of a death, by the Hebrew calendar, is called a yahrzeit, a Yiddish word meaning a year's time. On that day many Jews light a candle that burns for a whole day, say the mourner's Kaddish, give charity, and sometimes study in the person's memory. Some communities mark Aaron's own yahrzeit on the first of Av. A death is not just an event in the story; it's a day that comes back, and the Torah gives the first one.
screen: `THE FORTIETH YEAR, FIFTH MONTH, FIRST DAY.` · `NO DATE FOR MOSES IN THE TORAH.` · `THE FIRST OF AV.` · `YAHRZEIT: A YEAR'S TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: mark a date that matters to you. Settle, and breathe. Think of a date that holds someone: the day a grandparent died, the day a friend was born, the day you got sober, the day a child came home. Picture that person or that moment. If you keep a calendar, decide to put the date in it, so it comes back each year. If you pray, you might think of them by name when it comes. If not, simply hold them for a few breaths now. Stay with them until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Masei. The journeys. In the middle of the list, the Torah stops to give one exact date of death: Aaron's, on the first of Av.
Your line: dates are remembered. Today, put one date that matters into your calendar as a yearly reminder, and add the name it belongs to. Day four hundred seventy-seven.

478.title: Masei: cities of refuge (Numbers 35:9–15)
478.hook: six cities where one who killed by accident could flee
478.howItsDone: The cities of refuge are read in the portion of Masei in midsummer, and their laws are studied in the Talmud tractate Makkot, which describes the roads, signs and care for those who fled there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Torah paused its list of journeys to give one exact date of death, Aaron's, on the first of Av. Your line was dates are remembered. Whose date did you mark? Day four hundred seventy-eight.

A second of distraction on a wet road. A ladder that wasn't tied down. An accident that ends a life, and nobody meant it. In the ancient world, that wasn't the end of the story. A relative of the person who died might come looking for blood, and many societies expected him to. The Torah doesn't pretend that anger away. But as the people stand at the edge of the land, it sets aside something no one had asked for: six cities, built for the person who did the worst thing they never meant to do.
screen: `AN ACCIDENT, AND NOBODY MEANT IT.` → `A RELATIVE COMES LOOKING.` → `SIX CITIES SET ASIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the law, in paraphrase. When you cross the Jordan, choose cities to be cities of refuge, so that someone who kills a person by accident can flee there. Six in all: three east of the Jordan, three in the land of Canaan. And they're open to everyone: to Israelites, and to the stranger and the settler living among them. The Hebrew is ir miklat, a city of refuge, of shelter. The person who fled there was safe from the avenger, and would have a proper trial. If the death was found to be an accident, they lived in the city of refuge until the death of the high priest, and then they could go home. The rabbis took this law and made it humane in surprising detail. The Talmud says the roads to the cities had to be kept in good repair, and at every crossroads a sign was posted reading refuge, refuge, so that a frightened person running for their life would never take a wrong turn. The cities had to have water and markets, and be neither too small nor too crowded. If a student had to flee there, the Talmud says, his teacher went with him, so he wouldn't be cut off from learning. And the mothers of the high priests, it says, brought food and clothing to the people in the cities, so they wouldn't pray for the high priest to die. None of this pretends the death didn't happen. The person still lived away from home for years. But a mistake didn't have to end in another death. There was a road, signposted, to somewhere safe.
screen: `IR MIKLAT: A CITY OF REFUGE.` · `SIX CITIES, OPEN TO THE STRANGER.` · `REFUGE, REFUGE, AT EVERY CROSSROADS.` · `A TEACHER GOES WITH HIS STUDENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make room for someone's mistake. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who did something that hurt you, or hurt others, without meaning to. A careless word, a dropped responsibility, an honest mistake with real consequences. Notice the part of you that wants them to pay. Let it be there. Then ask: is there a road to refuge I could leave open for them? Not pretending it didn't happen, but not chasing them either. Picture a small sign at the crossroads. Breathe with it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Masei. The portion that sets aside six cities of refuge, open to Israelite and stranger alike, for those who killed by accident.
Your line: a place of refuge. Today, when someone admits a mistake to you, make your first words ones that leave them somewhere safe to stand. Day four hundred seventy-eight.

479.title: Masei: the land is shared (Numbers 35:33–34)
479.hook: bloodshed pollutes the land in which God dwells
479.howItsDone: These verses close the laws of homicide in Masei, read in midsummer, and Jewish law draws from related verses the principle of bal tashchit, avoiding needless destruction.

segments.voice: Yesterday, six cities of refuge, with signs at every crossroads reading refuge, refuge. Your line was a place of refuge. Did you leave someone a safe place to stand? Day four hundred seventy-nine.

Some places hold what happened in them. People stop wanting to live in a house after something terrible happens there. A street corner gets flowers and candles for years. We feel, even if we can't explain it, that ground remembers. After the cities of refuge, the Torah finishes its laws about killing with two verses that say exactly that. They aren't about the person who killed, or the family who grieves. They're about the land itself, and who else lives on it.
screen: `A HOUSE NOBODY WANTS TO LIVE IN.` → `FLOWERS ON A STREET CORNER.` → `THE GROUND REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Here are the verses, mostly in paraphrase. Don't pollute the land you live in, the Torah says, because blood pollutes the land, and the land can't be cleansed of blood shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it. Then the last line: don't defile the land you live in, where I dwell, and in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "for I the LORD dwell in the midst of the children of Israel." Notice the turn. It isn't only your land. It's a land with Someone else living in it too. Elsewhere, in Leviticus, God says it even more plainly: the land is Mine, and you are like strangers and settlers with Me. You're not the owners. You're the tenants, sharing a house with its owner. That changes the picture. Violence isn't just a crime between two families; it stains a shared home. The rabbis took it seriously. An early midrash says that bloodshed defiles the land and causes the Divine Presence to withdraw from it. The chapter itself, a few verses earlier, refuses any ransom for a murderer's life: no payment buys a way out. And the idea that the land itself can be harmed, and that we answer for it, has stayed in Jewish thought. Later teachers drew from other verses a law against needless destruction, called bal tashchit, starting with not cutting down fruit trees in war. The land is shared: with each other, with those who come after, and, the Torah says, with God.
screen: `BLOOD POLLUTES THE LAND.` · `I DWELL IN THE MIDST.` · `THE LAND IS MINE: YOU ARE TENANTS.` · `BAL TASHCHIT: DON'T DESTROY NEEDLESSLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for one piece of earth. Settle, and breathe. Think of a small patch of ground you have something to do with: a yard, a window box, a park bench you walk past, the strip of grass outside your building. Picture it as a shared home, shared with neighbors, with animals, with people who'll come after you, and, if you believe it, with God. What's one small thing you could do for it this week? Pick up litter, water something, plant something. Breathe with it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Masei. The portion whose laws end by saying blood pollutes the land, because God dwells in the midst of it.
Your line: the land is shared. Today, leave one piece of shared ground a little better than you found it. Day four hundred seventy-nine.

480.title: Numbers close: chazak
480.hook: the people stand on the plains of Moab, at the edge of the land
480.howItsDone: When the last verse of Numbers is read in synagogue, usually at the end of the double portion Matot-Masei in midsummer, the congregation calls out chazak, chazak, v'nitchazek, and the reader repeats it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Torah said blood pollutes the land, because God dwells in the midst of it. Your line was the land is shared. What piece of ground did you leave better? Today, the last verse of Numbers. Day four hundred eighty.

The night before a move, the boxes are packed and the rooms echo. You're not in the old life anymore, and not yet in the new one. You can see the truck, but you haven't driven anywhere. The book of Numbers ends right there. It began in the wilderness of Sinai, at the foot of the mountain, with a count of every person by name. It ends on the plains of Moab, beside the Jordan, across from Jericho. The river is right there. Nobody has crossed it yet.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE A MOVE.` → `IT BEGAN AT SINAI.` → `IT ENDS ON THE PLAINS OF MOAB.`

segments.voice: The very last story in Numbers is a small one, and it brings back old friends. The leaders of the tribe of Manasseh come to Moses with a worry about Zelophehad's daughters, the five sisters who won the right to inherit. If they marry into another tribe, the land goes with them, and the tribe's share shrinks. Moses answers, in paraphrase: the tribe speaks right too. The daughters may marry whomever they choose, as long as it's within their father's tribe. And they do. The book ends with a fair compromise, both sides heard. Then the final verse, in paraphrase: these are the commandments and the laws that the Lord commanded through Moses to the children of Israel, on the plains of Moab, by the Jordan, at Jericho. Think how far the book has come. It opened with a census of a generation that left Egypt. Nearly all of that generation is gone now, through the spies, the rebellions, and forty years of walking. A second census, back in Pinchas, counted their children. Miriam and Aaron have died. Moses knows he won't cross. The people standing on the plains of Moab are mostly people who were born in the desert or were children when they left. The wilderness book is over. And so, when the reader in synagogue finishes the last verse of Numbers, the congregation calls out the words said at the end of each book of the Torah: chazak, chazak, v'nitchazek. Be strong, be strong, and let us strengthen one another. Here it lands differently from the end of Leviticus. This time, everyone is standing at a river.
screen: `THE TRIBE SPEAKS RIGHT TOO.` · `ON THE PLAINS OF MOAB.` · `A NEW GENERATION AT THE RIVER.` · `CHAZAK, CHAZAK, V'NITCHAZEK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say chazak for finishing Numbers. Settle, and breathe. Let a few moments from this wilderness book come back to you: counted by name, the priestly blessing, the fish they missed, the spies who felt like grasshoppers, Korach, the rock, a donkey who saw first, five sisters, every stop on the road. Let one of them stay. Then, aloud or under your breath, say the three words: chazak, chazak, v'nitchazek. If someone you know is standing at the edge of something new, say it for them too. The bell holds the time.
Numbers close. The wilderness book ends on the plains of Moab, at the edge of the land, and the people say: be strong, be strong, and let us strengthen one another.
Your line: at the edge. Today, name one thing in your life that's almost about to begin, and take one small step toward the river. Day four hundred eighty.

481.title: These are the words
481.hook: Deuteronomy is Moses' farewell speech, retelling forty years
481.tomorrow: Devarim: the man of few words speaks
481.howItsDone: Deuteronomy is read in synagogue from midsummer to early fall, ending on Simchat Torah, and its first portion, Devarim, is read on the Sabbath before Tisha B'Av, or on the day itself when Tisha B'Av falls on the Sabbath and the fast is postponed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the book of Numbers ended on the plains of Moab, a new generation at the river, and we said chazak. Your line was at the edge. What's about to begin for you? Today, a new book. Day four hundred eighty-one.

People near the end of their lives often want to tell their stories. Not the whole thing, start to finish, but the parts that mattered, told their way, to the people who'll go on without them. Grandparents do it at the kitchen table. Teachers do it in a last lecture. The fifth book of the Torah is that, on the largest scale. Moses has a few weeks left. The people are camped across from the land he will never enter. And he begins to talk.
screen: `THE PARTS THAT MATTERED.` → `A FEW WEEKS LEFT.` → `AND HE BEGINS TO TALK.`

segments.voice: The book opens, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "These are the words which Moses spoke unto all Israel beyond the Jordan." In Hebrew, Eleh ha-devarim. These are the words. And that gives the book its Hebrew name: Devarim, words. The English name, Deuteronomy, comes from the old Greek translation and means something like second law, from a phrase inside the book about a copy of the teaching. The rabbis sometimes called it Mishneh Torah, the repetition of the Torah. Both names catch something. Much of what Moses says, we've heard before: the Ten Commandments, the spies, the golden calf, laws about festivals and justice. But this time it's not the narrator telling it. It's Moses, mostly speaking in his own voice, to a generation that was too young to remember, or wasn't born yet. And memory isn't a recording. When Moses retells the spies, for example, he says it was the people who first asked to send them, a detail that isn't in the version we read in Numbers. This is the story as he lived it, and wants them to keep it. The book opens on the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year. By the end of it, Moses has died. Jewish tradition counts the time between as only a few weeks. So the whole book is a farewell: one long last conversation. A new part of the path begins here, portion by portion through Moses' last words. Before anything else, notice the frame. The final thing the Torah gives us is a person speaking to the people he loves.
screen: `ELEH HA-DEVARIM: THESE ARE THE WORDS.` · `DEUTERONOMY: A SECOND TELLING.` · `THE STORY AS MOSES LIVED IT.` · `ONE LONG LAST CONVERSATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write a short farewell to something. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're leaving behind, or already have: a home, a job, a season of life, a habit, someone who has died, even a younger version of yourself. If you have paper, write three or four lines to it. What did it give you? What do you want to remember? What would you say if you could? If you don't have paper, compose the lines in your mind. Let them be simple and true. Breathe with them until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Devarim. Words. The Hebrew name of Deuteronomy, the book of Moses' farewell, from its opening line: these are the words.
Your line: last words matter. Today, when you say goodbye to someone, even for an afternoon, make the last thing you say a kind one. Day four hundred eighty-one.

screen: `DAY 481 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DEVARIM: THE MAN OF FEW WORDS SPEAKS.`

482.title: Devarim: the man of few words speaks (Deuteronomy 1:1)
482.hook: the one who said he was no man of words now speaks a whole book
482.howItsDone: Jewish communities begin reading Deuteronomy in the synagogue each summer with the portion Devarim, which is always read on the Sabbath just before Tisha B'Av.

segments.voice: Yesterday the last book of the Torah opened: Devarim, Moses' farewell. Your line was last words matter. Did you write your small goodbye to something? Today, a look at who is doing the talking. Day four hundred eighty-two.

Go back forty years, to a bush on fire in the desert. God tells a shepherd to go to Pharaoh, and the shepherd argues. In the old Jewish translation of Exodus he says, "I am not a man of words." He's slow of speech, he says, slow of tongue. Send someone else. God sends his brother Aaron along to do the talking. Now jump to the edge of the Jordan. The shepherd is an old man of a hundred and twenty. And the book that opens today is almost entirely him, talking. Speech after speech, for an entire book.
screen: `I AM NOT A MAN OF WORDS.` → `AARON DOES THE TALKING.` → `FORTY YEARS LATER: A WHOLE BOOK.`

segments.voice: The book begins: "These are the words which Moses spoke unto all Israel." In Hebrew, eleh ha-devarim. Devarim means words, and the book takes its Hebrew name from that opening, the way every book of the Torah does. The rabbis heard the irony right away. A midrash, in Deuteronomy Rabbah, sets the two verses side by side: the man who said I am not a man of words, and these are the words. Before, he couldn't speak. Now he speaks a whole book. What changed? The midrash's answer is that living with the Torah healed his tongue. Another way to hear it: forty years happened. He led a people who complained, he lost his sister and his brother, he broke tablets and carved new ones. When you've carried that much, you have something to say, and you stop worrying whether you say it beautifully. Look at what the speeches actually are, too. Moses isn't reading out new laws in a vacuum. He's retelling the journey to a generation that mostly wasn't there for the start of it, their parents having died in the wilderness. The book's Greek name, Deuteronomy, means second law, and the rabbis also called it Mishneh Torah, the repetition of the Torah. A retelling. Old stories told again, by someone who's earned the right to tell them. So the book of words belongs to the man who once had none. They didn't come from talent. They came from time.
screen: `ELEH HA-DEVARIM: THESE ARE THE WORDS.` · `THE MAN WHO SAID HE HAD NONE.` · `FORTY YEARS TO CARRY.` · `A SECOND TELLING, NOT A NEW ONE.` · then, large: `WORDS COME WITH TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing you've been too shy to say. Settle, and breathe. Think of a meeting, a dinner table, a group chat where you usually stay quiet. Is there one thing you know, or think, or need, that you haven't said because you worry it will come out wrong? Let it form in your mind as a single plain sentence. Not eloquent. Just true. Say it to yourself a couple of times until it sounds like you. Then decide where today it could be said out loud. The bell holds the time.
Devarim. Words, or things spoken. The Hebrew name of Deuteronomy, from its opening line, these are the words.
Your line: words come with time. Today, speak up once, in a place where you'd normally stay quiet. Plain is fine. Day four hundred eighty-two.

483.title: Devarim: small and great alike (Deuteronomy 1:17)
483.hook: judges must hear the small as the great and fear no one
483.howItsDone: Jewish law holds judges to equal care for every case regardless of its value or the parties' standing, and the Talmud's rule that a penny case is as precious as a fortune is still cited in teaching about Jewish courts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the man who once said he had no words began a whole book of them. Your line was words come with time. Did you speak up somewhere? Today, Moses remembers the judges he appointed. Day four hundred eighty-three.

Picture a desk at a city office. Two people in line. One is a well-known developer with a lawyer at his elbow and a building permit worth millions. The other is a retired woman whose neighbor's tree is dropping branches on her car. Whose file gets opened first? Whose gets read carefully? Everyone knows how it usually goes. Early in his farewell, Moses remembers the day he set up the first courts in the wilderness, and the charge he gave the judges. It's about exactly that line at that desk.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE IN LINE.` → `THE BIG FILE AND THE SMALL ONE.` → `MOSES CHARGES THE JUDGES.`

segments.voice: The charge, in the old Jewish translation, says: "ye shall hear the small and the great alike; ye shall not be afraid of the face of any man; for the judgment is God's." Three pieces. First, small and great alike. The rabbis took that literally, about money. The Talmud, in Sanhedrin, says a case over a single perutah, the smallest copper coin, must be as precious to the judge as a case over a hundred maneh, a fortune. Same care. Same patience. Same order in the line. Second, don't be afraid of the face of any man. A judge will someday face someone powerful, someone who could ruin them, someone with friends. The verse says: don't look away from the case to look at the face. And the reason is the third piece: the judgment is God's. The judge isn't the owner of justice, just the one holding it for a while, and answerable for how it was held. Notice who is listening to this speech. Not judges, mostly. A whole people. Moses is retelling it to everyone, because everyone ends up judging something: whose complaint gets heard at work, which kid's version of the fight gets believed, whose message gets answered tonight and whose waits a week. The small and the great show up at all of those desks.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give a small concern full attention. Settle, and breathe. Think of something small someone brought you lately that you brushed past. A kid's worry, a coworker's minor complaint, a parent's repeated question. Hold it up the way you'd hold a big one. What were they actually asking for? What would full attention have looked like? Let yourself feel the size it was to them. Then decide how you'll return to it today. The bell holds the time.
Devarim. Words, the name of this last book, where Moses retells even the charge he gave the first judges.

Your line: small and great alike. A week of edges: a date remembered, a city of refuge, a land that's shared, the edge of the Jordan, and now the words. Today, answer one small request as if it were a big one. Day four hundred eighty-three.
